title: The Eucharistic fast
hook: one hour without food before communion

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mass intentions: one name held up inside the whole Mass, and an offering that's a gift, not a price. Your line was a mass for them. Whose name did you write down? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five.

Sunday, a quarter past nine. Mass is at ten. In the kitchen, someone reaches for a granola bar, stops, glances at the clock on the stove, and does a bit of arithmetic. Communion comes partway through. So: is there time? Coffee, yes or no? A glass of water is fine, isn't it? It's a small, slightly comic moment, repeated in Catholic kitchens on Sunday mornings: grown adults doing math about a granola bar. But under the math is something serious. Why would the Church ask anyone to go a little hungry before receiving bread? Today, the Eucharistic fast.
screen: `A GRANOLA BAR AND A CLOCK.` → `MATH IN THE KITCHEN.` → `WHY GO A LITTLE HUNGRY?`

segments.voice: First, the rule itself, from the Church's law. Someone who is going to receive the Eucharist abstains from all food and drink for at least one hour before communion. Note the word: before communion, not before Mass. So the clock runs to the moment you receive, not to the opening hymn. Second, what's allowed. The same law sets aside water and medicine. Water doesn't break the fast. Pills don't break it. And the law adds something gentle: the elderly, the sick, and the people who care for them may receive communion even if they've eaten something within the hour. The rule bends toward the people who need it to bend. Third, why. Jesus says in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall not hunger." The fast is a small way of letting the body take part in that sentence. A little emptiness makes the bread stand out. It marks this food as different from breakfast, and it gives a short stretch of time, in the car, in the pew, to want what you're about to receive. Last, how small it is. One hour isn't heroic. That's partly the point. It's a fast sized for families with toddlers, for shift workers, for anyone. And because it's small, it's easy to forget, which is why the granola-bar arithmetic happens at all. The question under the arithmetic is a good one. Am I coming to this hungry? Or am I coming full, and distracted, and not really expecting anything?
screen: `ONE HOUR BEFORE COMMUNION.` · `WATER AND MEDICINE ARE ALLOWED.` · `THE BREAD OF LIFE.` · `A SMALL FAST FOR ANYONE.` · then, large: `HE THAT COMETH TO ME SHALL NOT HUNGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep the hour, or a piece of it, right now. Settle, and breathe. Notice your body. Is there any hunger in it, or thirst? Don't fix it. Just notice where it sits. Then ask a plain question: what am I hungry for, underneath the food? Rest, company, forgiveness, quiet, a sense that things will be all right. Let the answer come without arguing with it. If you pray, you can offer that hunger to God. If you don't, simply stay with it, kindly, for the rest of the bell. The bell holds the time.
The Eucharistic fast. No food or drink for at least an hour before communion, with water and medicine allowed, and the sick, the elderly and their caregivers excused. Today's word.

Your line: hungry for him. Before the next Mass you go to, keep the hour on purpose. Or, today, wait a few minutes before one meal and notice what you're really hungry for. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Catholics in the Latin Church abstain from food and drink, except water and medicine, for at least one hour before receiving communion. The elderly, the sick and those caring for them are excused.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't eat right before Mass, for some reason.
what it means: abstain from food and drink for at least an hour before communion, so the bread stands out and the body takes part in the waiting.
what a scholar hears: canon 919 counts the hour to communion, excepts water and medicine, and excuses the elderly, the infirm and those who care for them.

sources.quoted: I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall not hunger

notes: Canon 919 paraphrased: §1 abstain for at least one hour before holy communion from any food and drink, except only water and medicine; §3 the elderly, the infirm and those who care for them can receive even if they have eaten within the preceding hour. Confirm.
Eastern Catholic Churches have their own disciplines for the Eucharistic fast; the howItsDone says 'the Latin Church' for that reason. A Keeper may want a line on this in the teach.
Older, longer forms of the fast (e.g. from midnight) are deliberately not mentioned, under the claims rule.
The hook's timings (Mass at ten, communion perhaps forty minutes in) are illustrative.
Original: 'ieiunium eucharisticum' as the Latin term; confirm form and pronunciation.
